all.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

concepts.name: virtual reality
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.

The early era in the historical evolution of virtual reality (VR) is the period before modern digital computers were developed in the 1940s, and although not everything was present in that era, a few key developments were conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences.

In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

The flight simulator concept introduced for the first time in 1928 by Edwin A. Link evolved into sophisticated flight simulators with multiple sensors that provide an immersive experience, and this early development is considered a precursor to modern multi-sensory immersive virtual reality (VR).

The main objective of any virtual reality (VR) system is to let the user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer, not only for sight and sound but for all sensory organs.

There are broadly two major issues in experiencing virtual reality (VR): the technological issue of how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment, and the psychological issue of how to perceive those stimuli suitably, a human-factor issue that technology does not address and that is likely to differ between users.

The technological and psychological issues in virtual reality (VR) give rise to two major concerns that appear in almost every literature on VR technology or experience, namely immersion and presence.
The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

Cyber sickness can be independent of age when users view general virtual reality (VR) content, while age may be a factor for controllable content, making the age relationship clearer for controllable content.

A possible reason for increased cyber sickness among female head-mounted display (HMD) users is inter-pupillary distance (IPD) fit, because IPD determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit; this implies virtual reality (VR) displays should have a wider IPD adjustable range for female users.

Virtual reality (VR) recreates realistic movement and visual environments, making the user feel as if in a real-world environment; therefore, users with motion sickness (MS) susceptibility tend also to have cyber sickness susceptibility.

Prior exposure to virtual reality (VR) systems and repeated exposure to VR can reduce the effect of motion sickness (MS) susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time, so the positive correlation may not hold if either or both conditions are satisfied.

A user's physical position affects cyber sickness susceptibility: using a virtual reality (VR) system in a standing posture is likely to induce more cyber sickness, or more severe cyber sickness, than using the same system while sitting.

A virtual reality (VR) system is designed to create interactions that make the user feel immersed, and the amount of presence and the quality of the overall experience depend on fooling the user's perceptual system into believing the virtual system is the familiar real world.
Virtual reality generally provides the brain with sensory signals that are inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.

One possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body adapts to the new stimuli, making the user unaware of any flaws in the system and causing the user to believe that the virtual system is the real world rather than an artificial system.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.
An understanding of human perception is needed to design a better virtual reality (VR) system or to identify and resolve flaws in a given system.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: presence
concepts.definition: Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.

defining_facts.text: Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.

Presence is defined by the International Society for Presence Research, which has had the definition since 2000, as a psychological state or subjective perception in which part or all of an individual's current experience is generated by or filtered through human-made technology, but part or all of the individual's perception fails to accurately acknowledge the role of the technology in the experience.

Presence is a state in which computer-generated stimuli stimulate the user's sensory organs, and the user's perception is as good as perceiving reality because the user cannot distinguish those stimuli from real-world stimuli, so the user perceives them as coming from the real world rather than from a computer.

Presence is a state of consciousness or psychological sense of being in the virtual environment that exists inside the user's mind, has no direct manifestation, is difficult to measure objectively, and therefore requires the user's subjective experience to be taken into account.

Presence can be a function of both the user's subjective experience and a system's immersion, that is the objective or technological experience, so immersion can aid an enhanced perception of presence and is capable of producing presence, but it does not ensure presence.

Presence can be limited by immersion, and the greater the immersion a system or application provides, the greater the potential for a user to feel present in the virtual world, while the lesser the immersive technology provides, the lesser the presence.

The overall goal of any virtual reality system is to create a high degree of presence, that is to make users feel that they are really in the virtual world and unable to distinguish the real world from the virtual world.
Creating a high degree of presence in a virtual reality system requires the system to provide a high degree of immersion, and this requirement is a systemic issue.

The goal of any virtual reality (VR) system is to create a high degree of presence, meaning that people believe they are in the real world while they are actually in a virtual world, and the closer a VR system is to this goal, the better the immersive experience it provides.

Cybersickness (CS) mitigation involves a trade-off between reducing cybersickness and preserving user experience, because mitigation strategies often affect presence or the user's ability to perceive the virtual world, and presence affects user experience.

Mark Weiser's quote that the most profound technologies are those that disappear and presence refer to the same thing: the technological aspect surrounding the user should disappear from the user's perception, and the goal is to build systems that do not make it apparent that the user is using a specialized technological product.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the interaction and the perceptual stimuli, the latter being the output generated by the system, are designed to create the best possible illusion of reality, not actual reality, in order to enhance presence, which is a sense of reality as if the user is in the real world.

Presence in a virtual environment requires both reinforcing the virtual experience as believable and developing attachment to that experience, and the auditory experience plays a very important role in increasing presence in the virtual environment.

The key concerns to be addressed in the Majuli Island virtual reality (VR) Tour are capturing both the tangible and intangible aspects of the island's cultural heritage, which is the broader objective, the user experience, specifically the extent to which users feel present in the virtual island, and minimizing the risk of cyber sickness while users explore the island.
Presence is a psychological state of mind that is measured by standard questionnaires.
The QEP questionnaire was used to measure presence, and it is a 2004 revised version of the standard presence questionnaire (PQ).

The presence measure used to evaluate the virtual tour of Majuli Island included involvement, interface quality, adaptation or immersion, and visual fidelity, and tangible and intangible reconstruction fidelity was additionally reported for participants who had previously visited Majuli Island.

The overall user presence ratings for the virtual tour of Majuli Island were involvement mean 5.65 (standard deviation 1.11, coefficient of variation 0.19), interface quality mean 4.37 (standard deviation 1.4, coefficient of variation 0.32), adaptation and immersion mean 5.4 (standard deviation 1.13, coefficient of variation 0.2), and visual fidelity mean 5.79 (standard deviation 0.93, coefficient of variation 0.16).

The presence ratings for participants who had previously visited Majuli Island were tangible and intangible reconstruction fidelity mean 5.68 (standard deviation 1, coefficient of variation 0.177), involvement mean 5.83 (standard deviation 1.05, coefficient of variation 0.18), interface quality mean 4.72 (standard deviation 1.36, coefficient of variation 0.33), adaptation or immersion mean 5.61 (standard deviation 1.15, coefficient of variation 0.22), and visual fidelity mean 5.94 (standard deviation 0.93, coefficient of variation 0.15).

The overall presence results for the virtual tour of Majuli Island were summarized as good presence, meaning that users felt reasonably well located within the virtual environment while virtually exploring Majuli Island.

concepts.name: cybersickness
concepts.definition: Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.

defining_facts.text: Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.

A large number of symptoms may indicate the onset of cybersickness (CS) or cybersickness itself, and common ones include nausea, headache, excessive sweating, dryness of mouth, fullness of stomach, vomiting or a tendency to vomit, dizziness, disorientation, fatigue, and strange hand-eye coordination in which coordination does not happen in the expected way, so if one or more of these symptoms occur during a virtual reality (VR) experience, cybersickness can be assumed to be happening or going to happen.
Cybersickness (CS) can be caused by many factors, not by a single factor.

Reducing the impact of cybersickness (CS) is very important for usability and acceptability of virtual reality (VR) systems because it greatly enhances overall user experience and makes virtual reality applications more appealing to a wider range of people.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.

A sensory mismatch in a virtual reality (VR) system may be insignificant if the user's brain can adapt, but for other users it can cause cybersickness, with symptoms such as fatigue, headache, dizziness, and nausea.

Cybersickness, also known as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR), and it is not a single-factor effect because a variety of factors can affect it.

The factors that can induce cybersickness are broadly divided into internal factors, which include the age of the user, the gender of the user, the user's susceptibility to motion sickness, the physical condition of the user, and the emotional condition of the user, and external factors, which include hardware factors such as display resolution, latency, latency jitter, type of display, and type of input, and virtual reality (VR) content factors such as visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.

Finding feasible solutions to reduce the impact of cybersickness while a user is experiencing virtual reality (VR) is important because it is supposed to greatly enhance overall user experience and make VR more appealing to a wider range of people.

Cybersickness mitigation strategies often come at the cost of presence because reducing cybersickness may make the user feel more in an artificial environment than in a real environment and less likely to obtain a proper immersive experience.

concepts.name: teleportation
concepts.definition: The type of transition, meaning how the scene changes from one field of view to another, is another aspect of locomotion that affects cybersickness (CS); teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement such as walking, running, and jumping.

defining_facts.text: The type of transition, meaning how the scene changes from one field of view to another, is another aspect of locomotion that affects cybersickness (CS); teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement such as walking, running, and jumping.

Teleportation in virtual reality (VR) is a locomotion operation in which a user can pull up a menu, point to a desired virtual location, and be sent to that location without making any physical movement.

Target selection-based locomotion techniques include teleportation, which instantly changes the virtual viewpoint from the current location to the target location, map dragging, in which the user fixes a location to move there instantly, and the jumper technique in cave-type systems.

Route planning-based locomotion is a selection-based locomotion technique in which the user selects a route to the target rather than only the endpoint; there may be multiple routes, and while moving through the selected route, different viewpoint changes make the user feel movement along a path, providing more granular control over travel and slightly more natural movement than target-based teleportation.

Teleportation-type movement in a virtual world can be the best choice for reducing overall exposure duration because it provides instantaneous movement between two points at maximum speed, but it is not a natural movement and may not always be a good approach when naturalness is required.

concepts.name: virtual reality tour
concepts.definition: Virtual locomotion techniques (VLTs), used to navigate or perform a virtual reality (VR) tour by moving from one point to another, are broadly categorized into walking-based techniques (full gait, partial gait, and gait negation techniques, involving physical walking), steering-based techniques, selection-based techniques, and manipulation-based techniques.

defining_facts.text: Virtual locomotion techniques (VLTs), used to navigate or perform a virtual reality (VR) tour by moving from one point to another, are broadly categorized into walking-based techniques (full gait, partial gait, and gait negation techniques, involving physical walking), steering-based techniques, selection-based techniques, and manipulation-based techniques.

Virtual reality (VR) tours are categorized into user-controlled tours, in which the user controls how and where to navigate using controllers or other input modalities, and system-controlled tours, in which the system or application controls the user's movement, often following a predetermined path or sequence of movements.

System-controlled virtual reality (VR) tours are often an effortless experience with reduced cognitive demands because the system decides how and where the user moves, allowing the user to concentrate more on the experience itself.
Lack of user involvement in system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tours makes them less realistic and defeats the purpose of presence because the user is unable to control the movement.

The objective of the Majuli case study is an immersive, interactive virtual reality tour in which visitors can experience the island's ecological heritage and tangible and intangible cultural heritage, and each information point reveals related information for interactive exploration.

concepts.name: wayfinding
concepts.definition: Navigation has two components: locomotion or travel, which is the motor component, and wayfinding.

defining_facts.text: Navigation has two components: locomotion or travel, which is the motor component, and wayfinding.
Wayfinding refers to location awareness, ascertaining a path through the environment to a desired destination, and transferring spatial knowledge to the real world.

Wayfinding is essentially a mental model, and the goal of wayfinding is to build a mental model or cognitive map of the surroundings and overall environment so that it is easier to locate oneself and identify a suitable path.

For a good immersive user experience in a complex virtual environment with many objects and different ways to reach targets, wayfinding support is essential; locomotion or travel support alone is not sufficient, and regardless of how many or how sophisticated the travel techniques are, without suitable wayfinding support the user cannot use them efficiently or effectively.
Landmark support for wayfinding uses obvious distinct non-mobile objects positioned in a given place, and a good landmark should be clearly visible from several different locations or viewpoints.

Map support for wayfinding can provide maps of the space or place, such as a copy of the virtual world map, where the term world means the virtual world rather than the real world, or a world in miniature display that can show the entire virtual world with objects at different points, the current position of the user, and different routes to different points.
Path following support for wayfinding can denote multiple paths through a single space by colors, so the user knows that there are different paths to reach a destination.

Breadcrumb support for wayfinding leaves a trail of markers along the path followed by predecessors, so users can recognize that a path has already been explored, avoid getting lost, and choose another path or destination to save time.
A compass or another direction indicator can support wayfinding by specifying directions in two-dimensional or three-dimensional space, and a compass can be designed and placed in the environment.

concepts.name: optic flow
concepts.definition: Optic flow is the speed at which the visual scene changes, and movement is perceived through this change in the view of the surroundings; in a virtual reality (VR) tour, user movement appears as a constantly changing scene.

defining_facts.text: Optic flow is the speed at which the visual scene changes, and movement is perceived through this change in the view of the surroundings; in a virtual reality (VR) tour, user movement appears as a constantly changing scene.

When the navigation in a system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour is assumed to be walking, the scene-change speed (optic flow) should match the user's actual, or typical, real-world walking speed rather than VR walking speed; otherwise the movement looks unrealistic because it may be too fast or too slow.

A more realistic system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour requires matching its optic flow to the user's instantaneous walking speed using a model of the user's typical walking behavior, because a constant optic flow is not very realistic as people rarely walk at constant speed.

The natural walking model for a system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour is intended to provide a realistic walking experience by displaying a visual speed, or optic flow (the rate at which scenes change in the virtual world), that matches the user's perceived instantaneous walking speed, producing the perception of movement.

concepts.name: visual gain
concepts.definition: The desired perceived scene-change speed, denoted v_visual or v_perceived, is computed by multiplying the visual gain g by the actual instantaneous walking speed v_actual, so v_visual = g × v_actual, where v_actual is the user's movement speed and is related to the instantaneous step frequency.

defining_facts.text: The desired perceived scene-change speed, denoted v_visual or v_perceived, is computed by multiplying the visual gain g by the actual instantaneous walking speed v_actual, so v_visual = g × v_actual, where v_actual is the user's movement speed and is related to the instantaneous step frequency.
The visual gain g is typically set to 2.10 because prior studies have identified that value as providing a good visual gain for natural walking behavior.

concepts.name: natural walking speed model
concepts.definition: The natural walking speed model was formed by multiplying computed natural walking behavior by a visual gain factor to let the user perceive natural walking.

defining_facts.text: The natural walking speed model was formed by multiplying computed natural walking behavior by a visual gain factor to let the user perceive natural walking.
The empirical study was carried out to confirm whether the natural walking speed model, described as instantaneous speed, enhances perceived realism compared with a constant average speed.

The empirical study used a virtual art exhibition environment experienced with an Oculus Rift, in which system-controlled navigation moved the user at constant speed or instantaneous natural walking speed through pictures, with a forced 10-second stop at each picture.

Each participant experienced both constant speed and instantaneous speed conditions in a randomized order, with breaks between the conditions, to avoid practice effect and bias in the subsequent data collection.

The study used two 1-to-10 rating scales, with 1 representing worst and 10 representing the best value, to rate level of realism and user preference, and speed with levels constant and instantaneous was the independent variable, with realism and preference as the dependent variables.

Box plots of the realism and preference ratings showed that instantaneous speed produced higher realism ratings and higher user preference than constant speed, and paired sample t-tests with a p-value of 0.05 showed these differences were statistically significant.
The instantaneous natural walking speed model is suitable for a realistic walking experience in controlled virtual reality (VR) tools and is likely to increase presence.

The instantaneous natural walking speed model alone does not address cyber sickness, and the question of how to minimize cyber sickness with only that model cannot be answered, so additional measures are required.
The first stage of the travel-time algorithm is to compute the time to travel between two directly connected nodes using the natural walking-speed model.
In the natural walking-speed model, perceived instantaneous walking speed is the visual gain of 2.1 multiplied by the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed (V act).
In the natural walking-speed model, f is the instantaneous step frequency and h is the height of the user.

After solving the integral with simplifications, rearrangements, and Fourier-series expansion up to n0, the travel-time estimate tau D for a directly connected vertex pair under the natural walking model is D/V naught times (3 - (16/pi^2) * sum_{k=1}^{n0} 1/(2k-1)^2).
V naught is a constant for a given height h, equal to 2.1 h^2 divided by (0.157 * 1.72^2 * 1.8^2), where h is the user's height.

never_defined.name: virtual world
never_defined.definition: To different people, hearing extended reality (XR), virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), or mixed reality (MR) may lead them to associate one or more of these terms with magical movie scenes such as those in Avatar, interactive video games, 3D or 4D movie-theater documentaries about extinct animals, a user wearing a headset that blocks vision and transports the user to a virtual world, which is the most common perception of VR, games such as Pokémon Go in which the real world is visible on a device screen and virtual objects that do not exist in the real world can also be seen on that screen, or visualizations of internal body structures such as a skeleton or veins.

never_defined.name: virtual object
never_defined.definition: To different people, hearing extended reality (XR), virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), or mixed reality (MR) may lead them to associate one or more of these terms with magical movie scenes such as those in Avatar, interactive video games, 3D or 4D movie-theater documentaries about extinct animals, a user wearing a headset that blocks vision and transports the user to a virtual world, which is the most common perception of VR, games such as Pokémon Go in which the real world is visible on a device screen and virtual objects that do not exist in the real world can also be seen on that screen, or visualizations of internal body structures such as a skeleton or veins.

never_defined.name: virtual environment
never_defined.definition: A non-immersive virtual reality (VR) system is a specific, limited class of computer application, not any computer application, that provides a computer-generated environment in which the user can control characters or activities while retaining control of the physical environment, and the virtual environment does not directly interact with the user.

never_defined.name: height
never_defined.definition: The severity of cyber sickness (CS) also significantly increases with larger height and faster speed in a virtual environment.

never_defined.name: terrain
never_defined.definition: The geometry and terrain of a virtual environment affect cybersickness (CS); when a user travels over regular bumps and irregular terrain, CS is more likely than when the same travel occurs over flat terrain without bumpy rides.

never_defined.name: exposure duration
never_defined.definition: Virtual reality (VR) exposure duration is an important factor in cybersickness (CS), and prolonged exposure through head-mounted displays (HMDs) leads to greater cybersickness.

never_defined.name: distance
never_defined.definition: Combining sound with vision or visual effects affects perception of properties of the virtual environment, such as size, volume, material, intensity, and distance, and although looking alone partly gives an idea of those properties, perception of them is reinforced when vision is augmented with auditory effects.

never_defined.name: virtual experience
never_defined.definition: Audio reinforces a virtual experience as believable, that is, as closer to reality and everyday experience, and vision coupled with audio helps create or increase an emotional connection with the virtual environment, which vision alone may not be able to achieve.

never_defined.name: weight
never_defined.definition: The overall goal of haptic exploration is to integrate somatosensory signals from in-hand manipulation of an object so that a geometric mental model of the object is learned in terms of properties such as shape, size, weight and hardness.

never_defined.name: path
never_defined.definition: Wayfinding refers to location awareness, ascertaining a path through the environment to a desired destination, and transferring spatial knowledge to the real world.

never_defined.name: mental map
never_defined.definition: The global map and the local minimap support wayfinding and orientation awareness by showing the entire world in miniature; the minimap provides dynamic spatial orientation awareness about which direction to move, helping users create a mental map and wayfind.

never_defined.name: instantaneous step frequency
never_defined.definition: The desired perceived scene-change speed, denoted v_visual or v_perceived, is computed by multiplying the visual gain g by the actual instantaneous walking speed v_actual, so v_visual = g × v_actual, where v_actual is the user's movement speed and is related to the instantaneous step frequency.

never_defined.name: perception of movement
never_defined.definition: The natural walking model for a system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour is intended to provide a realistic walking experience by displaying a visual speed, or optic flow (the rate at which scenes change in the virtual world), that matches the user's perceived instantaneous walking speed, producing the perception of movement.

never_defined.name: experience optimization
never_defined.definition: The natural walking model for a system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour does not provide anything related to experience optimization; it can only be used to enhance presence in the virtual world.

never_defined.name: virtual reality navigation experience
never_defined.definition: The approach to optimizing virtual reality (VR) navigation experience that uses the natural walking model addresses cyber sickness by controlling the duration of exposure in the virtual world.

never_defined.name: virtual reality environment
never_defined.definition: In a virtual reality (VR) environment, cyber sickness is correlated with exposure duration, with the degree of the symptoms rising proportionally as the VR session duration increases, so if possible, shorter exposure duration can help eliminate or at least minimize the onset of cyber sickness.

never_defined.name: virtual reality exposure duration
never_defined.definition: The duration of virtual reality (VR) exposure depends on the size of the virtual world, the travelling speed, the travelling time, and the interaction time spent inspecting, selecting, or manipulating virtual objects.

never_defined.name: virtual world size
never_defined.definition: The duration of virtual reality (VR) exposure depends on the size of the virtual world, the travelling speed, the travelling time, and the interaction time spent inspecting, selecting, or manipulating virtual objects.

never_defined.name: virtual travel speed
never_defined.definition: The duration of virtual reality (VR) exposure depends on the size of the virtual world, the travelling speed, the travelling time, and the interaction time spent inspecting, selecting, or manipulating virtual objects.

never_defined.name: interaction time
never_defined.definition: The duration of virtual reality (VR) exposure depends on the size of the virtual world, the travelling speed, the travelling time, and the interaction time spent inspecting, selecting, or manipulating virtual objects.

never_defined.name: virtual terrain
never_defined.definition: Manipulating the virtual terrain or adjusting the distances between points of interest (POIs) can reduce travel time and therefore exposure time, but arbitrary terrain changes prevent users from perceiving the true size and feel of the real space and can hamper their mental map and wayfinding in the virtual world.

never_defined.name: distance between points of interest
never_defined.definition: Manipulating the virtual terrain or adjusting the distances between points of interest (POIs) can reduce travel time and therefore exposure time, but arbitrary terrain changes prevent users from perceiving the true size and feel of the real space and can hamper their mental map and wayfinding in the virtual world.

never_defined.name: system-controlled virtual reality tool
never_defined.definition: In a purely system-automated or system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tool, users do not interact with virtual objects, so the interaction time required to interact with virtual objects can be ignored.

never_defined.name: system-controlled navigation scenario
never_defined.definition: A semi-interactive tour in virtual reality (VR) is a system-controlled navigation scenario in which travel is automatic, users may interact with objects after a navigation task is complete, and interaction is limited to a small set of objects at points of interest (POIs), while users cannot interact with other objects in the virtual environment.

never_defined.name: semi-interactive virtual tour
never_defined.definition: In a semi-interactive virtual tour, interaction time at each point of interest (POI) can be limited to an estimate in advance of the maximum time an average user needs to interact with that POI, after which the system automatically forces the user to move to another POI.

never_defined.name: weighted graph
never_defined.definition: The virtual world part of a virtual experience is represented as a weighted graph G = (V, E), where V is the vertex set of all points of interest (POIs) and E is the set of weighted edges between POIs, representing a top view of the virtual world.

never_defined.name: weighted edge
never_defined.definition: The virtual world part of a virtual experience is represented as a weighted graph G = (V, E), where V is the vertex set of all points of interest (POIs) and E is the set of weighted edges between POIs, representing a top view of the virtual world.

never_defined.name: vertex
never_defined.definition: For every pair of vertices v1 and v2 in the vertex set V, the assigned edge weight is the Euclidean distance between v1 and v2 if they are directly connected, and a very large number represented by the infinity symbol if they are not directly connected.

never_defined.name: euclidean distance
never_defined.definition: For every pair of vertices v1 and v2 in the vertex set V, the assigned edge weight is the Euclidean distance between v1 and v2 if they are directly connected, and a very large number represented by the infinity symbol if they are not directly connected.

never_defined.name: actual instantaneous realistic walking speed
never_defined.definition: In the natural walking-speed model, perceived instantaneous walking speed is the visual gain of 2.1 multiplied by the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed (V act).

never_defined.name: distance element
never_defined.definition: Because speed is dx/dt, the instantaneous time dt for a distance element dx is dx divided by 2.1 times the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed (V act), and the total travel time over a distance D between directly connected nodes is the integral from 0 to D of dx/(2.1 V act).

never_defined.definition: Because speed is dx/dt, the instantaneous time dt for a distance element dx is dx divided by 2.1 times the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed (V act), and the total travel time over a distance D between directly connected nodes is the integral from 0 to D of dx/(2.1 V act).

never_defined.definition: Because speed is dx/dt, the instantaneous time dt for a distance element dx is dx divided by 2.1 times the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed (V act), and the total travel time over a distance D between directly connected nodes is the integral from 0 to D of dx/(2.1 V act).

never_defined.definition: The shortest path lengths used for the hypothetical edges are well-defined because the graph used for the travel-time minimisation problem is connected.

never_defined.name: edge set
never_defined.definition: The algorithm takes the original graph G, with vertex set V and edge set epsilon, as input and produces the optimal time T and the path P of the minimum-time path that covers all vertices in G.

never_defined.name: cybersickness time threshold
never_defined.definition: The minimum travel time to cover all vertices, as computed by the algorithm that maps the original graph to a travelling salesman problem (TSP) instance, may still exceed the cybersickness time threshold when the terrain or virtual environment is large, so its purpose may be defeated in such cases.

never_defined.name: time limit
never_defined.definition: There are two approaches to minimizing the possibility of cybersickness in a virtual world: finding a path that covers all points of interest in minimum time, and finding a path that covers the maximum possible points of interest within a given time limit.

never_defined.name: optimum time
never_defined.definition: In the minimum-time approach, the computed travel times become the weights of a complete graph formed by adding hypothetical edges, and this complete graph is given as input to a travelling salesman problem (TSP) solver, which outputs the optimum time and optimal path.

never_defined.name: threshold
never_defined.definition: The minimum-time approach that covers all points of interest may still produce a travel time beyond the threshold beyond which cybersickness may occur, motivating the use of a time limit in the alternative path optimization approach.

never_defined.name: alternative path optimization approach
never_defined.definition: The minimum-time approach that covers all points of interest may still produce a travel time beyond the threshold beyond which cybersickness may occur, motivating the use of a time limit in the alternative path optimization approach.
